To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
increasing dietary CP content above NRC recommendations for MP content and DMI, and increasing dietary MP content by increasing the inclusion of SBCS, resulted in greater milk yield.

the addition of urea to a diet with 16% CP increased milk yield by 0.8 kg d-1 (p <  0.05) and that the addition of soybean and cottonseed meal increased milk protein yield by 0,1 kg d-1 and milk yield by 1,1 kg d -1, compared with a control diet with 16 % CP (Table 1).

the inclusion of 17.5% crude protein (CP) diets in lactating dairy cows, with the same degradable intake protein (DIP) and metabolizable protein (MP) levels recommended by the NRC (2000), can improve milk production, corrected milk fat and milk protein yield.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of increasing the crude protein content of diets for lactating cows above the recommendations of the NRC (2004) on milk production and nutrient digestibility.
the effect of the level of crude protein (CP) in the diet on the performance of lactating Holstein cows.
the effects of increasing the dietary CP content from the NRC (2000) recommendations on milk production, and the effects of the source of CP on milk production and milk components.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results obtained from this research are consistent with the results of previous studies.

the results of this experiment suggest that increasing crude protein in the diet to 17.5% above the NRC recommendations of 2001 (16%) for metabolizable protein and degradable protein for cows in early lactation may improve milk yield and milk protein yield.

the results of this experiment indicate that feeding diets with a higher CP level (above the recommended level of 16% CP) to lactating dairy cows, by increasing the supply of amino acids to the intestines, could increase milk production.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the addition of urea to diets for lactating cows at 16.5% CP, increased milk production and reduced milk protein concentration, but did not affect the yield of milk solids corrected for fat and protein.

the use of high quality forages, especially alfalfa and corn silage, in combination with soybean meal, cotton seed meal and urea, is an excellent way to produce a diet that is high in metabolizable protein and crude protein for the dairy cow.
increasing dietary CP above the NRC (2007) recommendation of 16% for lactating cows can increase lactation performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that

increasing the crude protein content of the diet above the NRC (2007) requirements for metabolizable and rumen degradable protein, using soybean and cottonseed meal, can increase milk production, corrected milk fat and milk protein.
the use of urea to increase crude protein content in dairy cattle rations may result in reduced milk production, while the use of soybean meal to increase crude protein may increase milk production.
the use of urea to increase crude protein content in diets for lactating dairy cows is not recommended.
